source: Selsam et al. (2018) Learning a SAT solver from single-bit supervision (NeuroSAT)
finding: A message-passing network trained only on a sat/unsat bit learns to classify small random formulas and to decode satisfying assignments.
numbers: Trained on SR(U(10,40)); tested on SR(40): 85% classification accuracy; decodes a solution for 70% of satisfiable problems (guesses sat on 73% of them). Almost never says sat on unsat.
limits: Small random problems only. Not competitive with real solvers. Authors saw 'no obvious path' to practical use.
agent_relevance: Learned pattern recognition can find solutions on small SAT. It is a guesser, not a prover.

source: Selsam et al. (2018) Learning a SAT solver from single-bit supervision (NeuroSAT)
finding: Test-time generalisation to larger formulas works by running more message-passing iterations than in training.
numbers: SR(200): solves 25% of satisfiable problems with 4x more iterations than trained; under 10% at the trained iteration count. On 4,888 larger satisfiable structured problems (2.5x more clauses), decodes solutions for 85% with 512 iterations; Survey Propagation converges on none.
limits: Only satisfiable instances; still small scale.
agent_relevance: More test-time compute helps a fixed learned procedure on SAT. Fits a 'think longer' budget idea.

source: Selsam et al. (2018) Learning a SAT solver from single-bit supervision (NeuroSAT)
finding: NeuroUNSAT, trained for unsat, learns to spot unsat cores rather than do general proof search.
numbers: 100% prediction accuracy on its test set (SRC(30, PP(3,2))); core literals cluster separately 98% of the time.
limits: Test sets built around planted cores, so it may exploit a generator-specific pattern.
agent_relevance: Unsat detection by core recognition is brittle outside the generator. Do not trust a learned 'no' without a proof.

source: Selsam and Bjorner (2019) Guiding high-performance SAT solvers with unsat-core predictions
finding: Periodically replacing CDCL variable activity with NeuroSAT unsat-core predictions (NeuroCore) raised solved counts on SATCOMP-2018.
numbers: 5,000 s timeout: neuro-minisat 205 vs minisat 187 (+10%); satisfiable 125 vs 109 (+15%); unsat 80 vs 78 (+3%). Glucose +11% (186 to 206), Z3 +6%. Private scheduling set: neuro-glucose +20% in 1 hour.
limits: Self-reported on competition data; model trained on other problems.
agent_relevance: Learned hints on top of a complete solver can help while keeping soundness. The guess goes in the heuristic, the proof stays in the solver.

source: Selsam and Bjorner (2019) Guiding high-performance SAT solvers with unsat-core predictions
finding: The authors' own correction: much of the SATCOMP gain came from periodic refocusing, not from NeuroSAT's signal.
numbers: After fixing a bug, rand-glucose (uniform random logits in [-1,1] in place of NeuroCore scores) solved the same number as neuro-glucose on SATCOMP-2018. On scheduling problems rand-glucose solved 2.5% fewer than glucose, while neuro-glucose solved 20% more.
limits: A real signal remains only on the in-distribution scheduling set. The authors say so.
agent_relevance: Always run a random-signal control. A 'learned guidance' gain can be a perturbation effect. Same lesson as our honest-control rule.

source: Selsam and Bjorner (2019) Guiding high-performance SAT solvers with unsat-core predictions
finding: Gains are concentrated on satisfiable instances, which suggests help with finding models rather than proving none exist.
numbers: neuro-minisat: +15% on satisfiable, +3% on unsatisfiable; lead appears within the first minutes and holds to the end (cactus plot).
limits: Single timeout, one run per solver.
agent_relevance: Learned guidance helps search for witnesses more than it helps exhaustive refutation.

source: Kurin et al. (2020) Can Q-learning with graph networks learn a generalizable branching heuristic for a SAT solver?
finding: Q-learning with a GNN branching policy (Graph-Q-SAT) cuts MiniSat decisions on random 3-SAT, but only in iteration counts.
numbers: Median iteration reduction vs MiniSat, trained on SAT-50-218: SAT-50-218 2.46x; SAT-100-430 3.94x; SAT-250-1065 3.91x. Unsat: 2.34x, 2.24x, 1.54x. Using the model for only the first 10 decisions still beats VSIDS.
limits: Authors say more work is needed to cut wall-clock time in modern settings. Random 3-SAT only. Gain falls on unsat at large size.
agent_relevance: Early good decisions matter while VSIDS warms up. Learned search policies cut steps but may cost more per step.

source: Kurin et al. (2020) Can Q-learning with graph networks learn a generalizable branching heuristic for a SAT solver?
finding: Policy trained only on satisfiable instances transfers to unsatisfiable ones and to 5x larger problems, with weaker gains.
numbers: Unsat median iteration reduction 2.34x (50 vars), 2.24x (100), 1.54x (250) vs 2.46x, 3.94x, 3.91x on SAT. Authors note the larger-size gain may reflect MiniSat scaling worse.
limits: Random 3-SAT only; one training setup.
agent_relevance: Search skill that prunes early (more propagations per decision, 6.62 vs 4.18) transfers, but refutation transfers less.

source: Li, Guo, Si (2024) G4SATBench: Benchmarking and advancing SAT solving with graph neural networks
finding: A fair benchmark of GNN SAT solvers finds good in-distribution accuracy but weak transfer.
numbers: Classification accuracy on easy sets about 93-99.99% (SR about 96%); on medium sets SR falls to about 66-78% and 3-SAT to about 83-85%. Across datasets and to larger formulas, NeuroSAT and GGNN struggle to generalise in most cases; training on SR generalises best.
limits: 7 problem families, 3 difficulty levels. Several seeds failed to train with some losses.
agent_relevance: Do not expect a learned satisfiability judge to transfer. Test on shifted distributions.

source: Li, Guo, Si (2024) G4SATBench: Benchmarking and advancing SAT solving with graph neural networks
finding: GNN solvers learn something like greedy local search, not CDCL backtracking.
numbers: Adding learned clauses to formulas lets GNNs trained on augmented data do much better, yet models trained on the original formulas fail on these instances, which CDCL solves in a few steps.
quote: GNNs may not implicitly learn the CDCL heuristic
limits: Interpretation is the authors' inference from probes.
agent_relevance: Learned systems do forward greedy guessing well and backtracking badly. A scaffold should supply explicit backtracking.

source: SATBench authors (2025) SATBench: Benchmarking LLMs' logical reasoning via automated puzzle generation from SAT formulas
finding: On 2,100 SAT-derived puzzles, accuracy falls as clause count rises, to near chance on hard instances.
numbers: Zero-shot: o4-mini 78.0% on hard (31-50 clauses) and 65.0% on hard UNSAT; average over all models on hard 53.0% (random 50%). Easy 4-19 clauses, medium 20-30. Hard averages: SAT 66.7% vs UNSAT 39.3%.
limits: Puzzles written by an LLM from formulas; human check of 100 puzzles passed about 93-100% per task. On hard, bigger models plateau around 50-53%.
agent_relevance: LLMs show satisfiability bias: they say 'sat' without a witness. Ask for a checkable assignment or refutation.

source: SATBench authors (2025) SATBench: Benchmarking LLMs' logical reasoning via automated puzzle generation from SAT formulas
finding: Right answers often come with invalid reasoning; errors are systematic.
numbers: Trace accuracy drops more on SAT than on UNSAT. Error types in the paper: condition omission (14.3% of o4-mini errors, 12.6% for DeepSeek-R1), context inconsistency, spurious priors. GPT-4o falls to near 50% at about 30 clauses.
limits: Judge is an LLM; error counts are for two models.
agent_relevance: Verify each clause explicitly. A trace check catches omitted constraints.

source: SATBench authors (2025) SATBench: Benchmarking LLMs' logical reasoning via automated puzzle generation from SAT formulas
finding: Naming failure patterns in the prompt helped more than light fine-tuning.
numbers: Making failure patterns explicit: 60.4% of o4-mini failures and 73.2% of DeepSeek-R1 failures corrected on re-evaluation. LoRA on 1,100 o4-mini traces, Qwen2.5-14B: 51.9% to 53.6%.
limits: Re-evaluation was on previously failed cases (selection effect). Fine-tune gain small.
agent_relevance: Error-aware checklists look more useful than fine-tuning on a small trace set.

source: Ye et al. (2023) SatLM: Satisfiability-aided language models using declarative prompting
finding: Having the LLM write a declarative spec and a solver (Z3) reason beats imperative program-aided LMs on constraint tasks.
numbers: code-davinci-002, greedy: GSM-SYS 69.4 vs PROGLM 43.4 vs CoT 46.5; LSAT 35.0 vs CoT 23.5; BoardgameQA 79.4 vs CoT 60.7; CLUTRR 68.3 vs 58.9; ProofWriter 99.7 vs 83.7. SOTA LSAT 30.9 to 37.4; BoardgameQA 73.9 to 80.7 (self-consistency).
limits: On plain GSM, SatLM is on par or slightly worse with greedy (71.8 vs 72.7); the gain needs self-consistency (82.4). Old model generation.
agent_relevance: Offload search to a solver and let the LLM only parse. Same split as our scaffold: model formalises, tool decides.

source: Ye et al. (2023) SatLM
finding: The solver gives built-in error signals (UNSAT, AMBIG) that raise selective accuracy at the cost of coverage.
numbers: Selective accuracy on GSM-SYS: SatLM 77% vs PROGLM 45%; SatLM answers fewer questions on all three datasets but wins overall on GSM-SYS and CLUTRR.
limits: Lower coverage; on GSM the gap only appears with several samples.
agent_relevance: A solver that says 'inconsistent' or 'underdetermined' is a free abstain and re-parse trigger (S4 TEST).

source: Hazra et al. (2025) Have large language models learned to reason? A characterization via 3-SAT phase transition
finding: LLMs show an easy-hard-easy curve over the clause/variable ratio, dropping to about 10% in the hard region. Few-shot examples do not help there.
numbers: Random 3-SAT, at most 10 variables and 110 clauses. Hard-region accuracy about 10% for non-reasoning LLMs; unchanged between 0-shot and 3-shot. Accuracy rises with the fraction of satisfying assignments.
limits: Tiny instances. Search and decision variants both tested.
agent_relevance: Failure when no statistical shortcut exists. Hard problems need real search or an external solver.

source: Hazra et al. (2025) Have large language models learned to reason? A characterization via 3-SAT phase transition
finding: DeepSeek-R1 is the exception: its hard-region accuracy beats other LLMs' easy-region accuracy and does not depend on satisfiability ratio.
numbers: R1 uses more thinking tokens in hard regions; near-perfect on 2-SAT and Horn-SAT. It detects satisfiable formulas soundly but often fails to find the assignment (incomplete).
quote: R1 shows signs of having learned the underlying reasoning
limits: Authors call R1's reasoning neither sound nor complete; scale is tiny versus solvers with thousands of variables.
agent_relevance: Reasoning models search, but incompletely. Authors advise search scaffolds with neurosymbolic tools.

source: Zhang, Chen, Chen (2026) Satisfiability solving with LLMs: a matched-pair evaluation of reasoning capability
finding: Plain accuracy overstates LLM SAT skill because models label nearly everything satisfiable.
numbers: Models fail to reproduce the easy-hard-easy signature and degrade sharply as variable count grows. A paired metric (ADR) needs both a satisfiable formula and its minimally edited unsatisfiable twin right; 'always predict SAT' gives accuracy 0.5 but ADR 0.
limits: 2-SAT and 3-SAT plus Vertex Cover and 3D packing reductions; some large-size runs had low completion.
agent_relevance: Test with matched sat/unsat pairs, not single items. Counter yes-bias directly in S4.

source: Zhang, Chen, Chen (2026) Satisfiability solving with LLMs: a matched-pair evaluation of reasoning capability
finding: A leading model is accurate on small formulas but scale breaks it; decisions agree across encodings.
numbers: GPT-5 ADR 0.79 at 25 variables, 0.35 at 50 (completion rate only about 20% at 50). Decisions on CNF and on reduced graph/packing forms agree on over 80% of instances for most models.
limits: The 50-variable point is an extra validation run, omitted from the main plot.
agent_relevance: Scale degradation is the main limit; track output completion as well as correctness.

source: Heule, Kullmann, Marek (2016) Solving and verifying the boolean Pythagorean triples problem via cube-and-conquer
finding: SAT solving settled a long-open Ramsey question with a checkable proof, showing why proof certificates matter.
numbers: Any 2-colouring of {1..7825} has a monochromatic Pythagorean triple. Cube-and-conquer: about 4 CPU years total (21,900 h splitting, 13,200 h solving); 800 cores about 2 days; DRAT proof almost 200 TB, verified; compressed certificate 68 GB; regenerating proofs about 13,000 CPU h, checking about 16,000.
limits: Huge compute; proof checked by tools, not human-readable.
agent_relevance: A 'no' from search is only trusted with a verifiable certificate. The shape of S4 for UNSAT claims.

source: Ozolins et al. (2022) Goal-aware neural SAT solver (QuerySAT)
finding: Letting the network try candidate assignments and see an unsupervised loss value improves neural SAT solving over NeuroCore.
numbers: On 3-SAT test (5-405 variables, 40k formulas) at the same time budget QuerySAT solves about 36k vs NeuroCore about 18k; NeuroCore plateaus near 40% accuracy after 16k steps; NeuroCore gets almost zero on 3-Clique, k-Coloring and SHA-1 tasks.
limits: Still behind classical solvers; trained at 32 steps.
agent_relevance: Query-and-check loops (try, get feedback, revise) beat one-shot guessing. Matches a test-in-the-loop operator.

source: NeuroBack authors (2023) NeuroBack: Improving CDCL SAT solving using graph neural networks
finding: One offline GNN query to predict variable phases gives modest gains on a strong solver, with a random-phase control.
numbers: Kissat on SATCOMP-2022: Default 193, Random-phase 197, NeuroBack 203 (+5.2% vs default, +3.0% vs random). SATCOMP-2023: Default 198, Random 190, NeuroBack 204 (+3.0% vs default, +7.4% vs random). Backbone classifier 75.1% accuracy. Average speed-up 53.2% on sat vs 14.6% on unsat instances.
limits: Gains of only 3-7%; random phase beat default in 2022, so the control matters.
agent_relevance: Cheap one-shot learned priors plus a complete solver; keep a random baseline.

source: SATLUTION authors (2025) SATLUTION: Autonomous code evolution meets NP-completeness
finding: LLM agents evolving whole C/C++ solver repositories beat SAT Competition 2025 winners on the authors' runs.
numbers: Solved counts: evolved top-3 solvers 347, 345, 344 vs gold AE_kissat2025_MAB 334 and silver kissat-public 331 (their hardware; official results 327 and 321). Started from 2024 codebases; about 70 evolution cycles; reward based on PAR-2.
limits: Self-reported, own hardware, not an official entry. Evolution used the 2024 benchmark.
agent_relevance: Strict correctness checks plus a hard metric let an LLM improve a mature tool. Verification is the enabler.

source: AutoModSAT authors (2025) Discovering heuristics in a complex SAT solver with LLMs (AutoModSAT)
finding: LLM-generated heuristic functions improve a modular CDCL solver, but part of a rival's gains is just parameter choice.
numbers: 40% better than baseline ModSAT, 30% better than its parameter-tuned version, over 30% average gain vs Kissat and CaDiCaL on 11 datasets (PAR-2, 10 seeds, 95% CI). Versus tuned Kissat/CaDiCaL it matches or exceeds solved count on 8 of 11. Tuned Kissat wins on Zamkeller; eliminate=0 and simplify=0 explain most of that.
limits: Baseline ModSAT is weaker than Kissat; AutoModSAT searches only 7 functions.
agent_relevance: Compare against a tuned baseline, not the default.

source: DaSAThco authors (2025) Data-aware SAT heuristics combinations optimization via LLMs
finding: Mapping instance features to heuristic ensembles generalises out of domain better than one tuned configuration, though a tuned single solver can still win in domain.
numbers: Timeout 1000 s. Exact PAR-2 numbers not extracted this session.
limits: Small benchmarks; only skimmed.
agent_relevance: Route by problem family rather than using one fixed recipe off-distribution.
